column4: ### Genesis: The God Who Dwells With His Creation
column5: ### Genesis: God Who Dwells with His Creation

column4: A central theme in the narrative of God is His **desire to dwell** with His creation. This is clear in the stories throughout Genesis. Across its fifty chapters and genealogies from Adam (the first man) through Joseph (that last major figure in the book of Genesis, the last significant leader of God’s people before Moses), there is a period of approximately ~2,400 years. We can see through these stories the consistency of God’s goodness despite man’s wickedness.

column4: The phrase **“I AM THAT I AM”** (Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh) is one of the most profound self-revelations in Scripture. When Moses asks for God’s name, God responds with this phrase, which can be translated as "I Am Who I Am," "I Will Be Who I Will Be," or simply "I Am." This declaration on the surface is a bit confusing but holds deep meaning. Could you imagine introducing yourself to someone new as ‘I am’? When God reveals Himself as ‘I AM THAT I AM’ He is attesting to His nature, His eternal presence, His sovereignty. ‘I am’ is infinite in meaning and purpose.

column4: In the ~1,400 years between the death of Moses and the birth of Christ the Israelites experienced a recurring cycle of devotion which brings God's favor and blessings, followed by rebellion, God’s judgment, their subsequent repentance, and ultimately God’s deliverance. This pattern is particularly evident in the books of **Judges, Kings, and Chronicles**, which recount cycles where the people turn away from God, often by worshiping other gods, resulting in periods of oppression or exile. In response to their cries, God repeatedly raised up judges, prophets, or leaders to deliver them.

column4: God’s character and actions are fully expressed in the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit. The scriptures teach that God is one in essence, yet exists as three distinct persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s oneness, stating, “beside Him there is no God” (Isaiah 45:5). However, the Godhead is understood as a **compound unity**-three distinct persons who cooperate with a singular mind and purpose, united in the truest sense. Each person of the Trinity has a unique role: the **Father creates**, the **Son redeems**, and the **Holy Spirit sanctifies**. The term “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible; it was developed as a theological expression to describe this concept, which is revealed through Scripture.
column5: God’s character and works are fully revealed in the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit. Scripture teaches that in essence God is one, yet exists as three distinct persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms the unity of God, saying, “There is no other God besides Me” (Isaiah 45:5). Even so, the Godhead is understood as a **compound unity**—three distinct persons who work together with one mind and purpose, united in the truest sense. Each person of the Trinity has a unique role: **the Father creates**, **the Son redeems**, and **the Holy Spirit sanctifies**. The word “Trinity” is not found in the Bible; it developed as a theological expression to explain this concept revealed through the Scriptures.

column4: The Trinity can be illustrated by examples in nature, which help clarify this idea of unity in diversity. Like water, which can be liquid, ice, or vapor but remains H₂O, each person of the Trinity is fully God yet distinct in personhood. Or consider a triangle, with three sides and three angles, forming one complete shape; if one side is removed, it ceases to be a triangle. Similarly, **God’s nature is incomplete without all three persons**, who work together in perfect unity.

column4: We can be uniquely known by our names: husband, father, son, brother, friend. Each of these a declaration of who we are in relation to someone else. We can also be known by our attributes: faithful, patient, kind, intelligent, funny. Likewise, we can know God by His attributes and names- He is our Healer, Provider, Shepherd, and Redeemer. However, as labels and words are only a small part of us, for ourselves to be truly known by others, we must be experienced. Even more so with God. To truly and fully know Him we must experience Him.
column5: We can be known in unique ways by our names: husband, father, son, brother, friend. Each of these is a declaration of who we are in relation to someone else. We can also be known by our attributes: faithful, patient, kind, wise, humorous. Similarly, we can know God by His attributes and names—He is our Healer, Provider, Shepherd, and Redeemer. However, just as labels and words are only small parts of us, in order for others to truly know us, we must be experienced. This is even more true of God. To truly and fully know Him we must experience Him.

column4: God’s names reveal His character, but personal encounters deepen our understanding of what these names signify. For instance, “God my Healer” takes on a richer, more profound meaning when we understand the depths of illness, desperation, or helplessness from which God rescues. Knowing Him as our Provider is transformed when we have felt true need and found Him faithful.

column4: Scriptures offer a context to these encounters, showing us God’s faithfulness to His people across time and circumstance, reinforcing how His names and attributes are not mere titles but realities He brings to life, experienced in the lives of individuals.
